# Quantile functions and order statistics {#sec-chap-quantiles}

So far we have seen several characterizations of probability distributions:
cumulative distribution functions (CDFs), Laplace transforms for distributions supported on $[0, \infty)$, characteristic functions. The last characterization is praised
for its behavior with respect to sums of independent random variables.

For univariate distributions, a companion to the cumulative distribution function  is the *quantile function*. It plays a significant role in simulations, statistics and  risk theory.


Recall that a cumulative distribution function $F$ is non-negative, $[0,1]$-valued, non-decreasing, right-continuous, with left-limit at any point. The cumulative distribution function of a diffuse probability measure
is continuous at any point.

## Definition {#sec-def-quantiles}

The quantile function $F^{\leftarrow}$ is defined as an extended/generalized inverse
of the cumulative distribution function $F$.

::: {#def-quantfun}

### Quantile function

The quantile function $F^{\leftarrow}$ of random variable  $X$
distributed according to $P$ (with cumulative distribution function $F$) is defined as
$$\begin{array}{rl}
F^{\leftarrow} (p)
   & = \inf \Big\{ x : P\{X \leq x\} \geq p \Big\} \\
   & = \inf \Big\{ x : F (x) \geq p \Big\} \qquad \text{for } p \in (0,1).
\end{array}$$

:::

We first  check that this definition makes sense, that is $F^{\leftarrow} (p) \in \mathbb{R}$ for every $p \in (0,1)$.
Indeed, we establish. 

::: {#prp-quantiles}

Let $F$ be the Cumulative Distribution Function of some probability distribution over $(\mathbb{R}, \mathcal{B}(\mathbb{R}) )$

For any $p \in (0,1)$,  $\inf \{x : F(x) \geq p\} \in \mathbb{R}$ and $\inf \{x : F(x) \geq p\}= \min \{x : F(x) \geq p\}$.

:::


::: {.proof}

For any $p \in (0,1)$,  the set $\{x : F(x) \geq p\}$ is non-empty. If it were empty, the sequence $(F(n))_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ would be bounded from above by $p$. 

Having $\inf \{x : F(x) \geq p\}=-\infty$ would contradict $\lim_{n \to \infty}F(-n)=0$.  Hence the infimum of $\{x : F(x) \geq p\}$ belongs to $\mathbb{R}$. Let $m$ denote this infimum. For $n \in \mathbb{N}$, let $t_n = m +1/n$. We have $F(t_n)\geq p$, otherwise $m$ would not be the infimum of $\{x : F(x) \geq p\}$. The sequence $(F(t_n))_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ converges to $F(m)$ (right-continuity of $F$) and the limit is lower bounded by $p$. Hence, $F(m) \geq p$, so $m \in \inf \{x : F(x) \geq p\}$.
This means:
$$\inf \{x : F(x) \geq p\}= \min \{x : F(x) \geq p\} \, .$$

:::

@prp-quantiles asserts that @def-quantfun is sound.

::: {#prp-quantile-properties}

A quantile function 

a. is non-decreasing, 
b. is left-continuous at every point in $(0,1)$. 
c. has a limit on the right at every point in $(0,1)$.

:::


::: {.proof}

a. Let $F$ be the Cumulative Distribution Function of some probability distribution over $(\mathbb{R}, \mathcal{B}(\mathbb{R}) )$. Let 
$F^{\leftarrow}$  be the associated quantile function. 

    If $0 <p \leq p' < 1$, $\{ t : t \in \mathbb{R} F(t) \geq p'\} \subseteq \{ t : t \in \mathbb{R} F(t) \geq p\}$, hence $F^\leftarrow(p') = \inf \{ t : t \in \mathbb{R} F(t) \geq p'\} \geq  \inf \{ t : t \in \mathbb{R} F(t) \geq p\} =F^\leftarrow(p)$.

b. To check left-continuity of $F^\leftarrow$, it is enough to check that for each $u \in (0,1)$, for each increasing sequence $(u_n)_n$ such that $\lim_n u_n = u$, we have $\lim_n F^\leftarrow(u_n) = F^\leftarrow(u)$.

    As $F^\leftarrow$ is non-decreasing, $(F^\leftarrow(u_n))_n$ is a non-decreasing sequence bounded above by $F^\leftarrow(u)$. Hence it converges to some limit $\ell \leq F^\leftarrow(u)$. 

    Suppose $\ell < F^\leftarrow(u)$. Then $F(\ell) < u$ as $F^\leftarrow(u)$ is the infimum of the set $\{x : F(x) \geq u\}$.

    But then $u_n > F(\ell)$ and $\ell < F^\leftarrow(u_n)$ for all $n$ large enough since $(u_n)_n$ is an increasing sequence converging to $u$, which contradicts the fact that $\ell$  is the monotone limit of $(F^\leftarrow(u_n))_n$. 

    Thus $\ell = F^\leftarrow(u)$.

c. To check the existence of the right-hand limit, it is enough to remember that a quantile function is non-decreasing. 
:::

Note that, as a non-decrasing function, a quantile function is always Borel-measurable. 

The interplay between the quantile and cumulative distribution functions is summarized in the next proposition.

::: {#prp-quantilekit}

If $F$ and $F^\leftarrow$ are  the cumulative distribution function and the quantile function of
(the distribution of) $X$, the following statements hold  for  $p \in] 0, 1 [$:

1. $p \leq  F (x)$ iff $F^\leftarrow (p) \leq  x$.
1. $F \circ F^\leftarrow (p) \geq p$ .
1. $F^\leftarrow \circ F (x) \leq  x$ .
1. If  $F$ is  continuous, then $F \circ F^\leftarrow (p) = p$

:::

::: {.proof}
According to the definition of $F^\leftarrow$ if $F (x) \geq p$ then $F^\leftarrow
(p) \leq  x.$

To prove the  converse, it suffices to check that $F \circ F^\leftarrow (p) \geq p$.

Indeed, if $x \geq F^\leftarrow (p),$ as
$F$ is non-decreasing $F (x) \geq F \circ F^\leftarrow (p)$. If $y = F^\leftarrow
(p),$ by definition of $y = F^\leftarrow (p),$ there exists a
non-increasing sequence $(z_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ which converges to $y$ such that
$F (z_n) \geq p .$ But as $F$ is right-continuous $\lim_n F
(z_n) = F (\lim_n z_n) = F (y) .$ Hence $F (y) \geq p$.

We just proved  1. and 2.

3.) is an immediate  consequence de 1). Let $p = F (x) .$ Hence
$p \leq  F (x),$ according to 1.) this is equivalent to  $F^\leftarrow (p)
\leq  x,$ that is  $F^\leftarrow \circ F (x) \leq  x.$

4.) For  $p$ in $] 0, 1 [,$  let $y = \inf \{ x :  F (x)\geq p \} =F^\leftarrow (p)$.
According to  $1)$,  $F (y) \geq p$. Now,  if $(z_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ is an increasing sequence
converging to  $y$, for every  $n$, $F (z_n) < p,$ and, by continuity,
$F (y) = F (\lim_n z_n) = \lim_n F (z_n) \leq
p.$ Hence $F (y) = p,$ that is  $F \circ F^\leftarrow (p) = p.$

:::

<br>

## Quantile functions and stochastic simulation {#sec-quantile-coupling}

::: {#prp-quatile-transformation}

### Quantile transformation

If $U$ is uniformly distributed on $(0,1)$, and $F$ is a cumulative
distribution over $\mathbb{R}$, $F^{\leftarrow}(U)$ has cumulative distribution $F$.

:::

::: {.proof}

$$\begin{array}{rl}
  P\Big\{ F^\leftarrow(U) \leq x \Big\}
  & = P\Big\{ U \leq F(x) \Big\} \\
  & = F(x) \, 
\end{array}$$
where the first equality follows from a) in @prp-quantilekit. 
  
:::



::: {#rem-quantile-transformation}

The quantile transformation works whatever the continuity properties of $F$.

:::

The quantile transformation has many applications. It can be used to
show stochastic domination properties. 
It can be used to build random generators once a uniform random generator is  avalaible. 

::: {#exm-exmples-quantiles}

In [Figures @fig-quantiles] up to  [@fig-quantiles4], we illustrate quantile functions for discrete (binomial)
distributions and for distributions that are neither discrete nor continuous. The quantile function
of a discrete distribution is step function  that jumps at the cumulative probability of every possible outcome.
If a probability distribution is a mixture of a discrete distribution and a continuous distribution, the
quantile function jumps at the cumulative probability of every possible outcome of the discrete component.

:::

```{r}
#| echo: false
#| message: false
#| warning: false
#| label: fig-quantiles
#|
#| fig-cap: |
#|    Quantile functions of binomial distributions.
#|
n <- 10
p <- seq(0, 1, by=.01)
probs <-  c(.2,  .5)

df <- as.data.frame(c(list("p"=p),
                      probs |> purrr::map(.f = function(prob) qbinom(p, n, prob))))

names(df) <- c("p", format(probs, digits=2))

df <- tidyr::gather(df, key="prob", value="quantile", -p)

p <- ggplot2::ggplot(data = df) +
     ggplot2::geom_step(mapping=ggplot2::aes(x=p, y=quantile, linetype=prob), color=1, direction = "hv", lineend="butt") +
     ggplot2::xlab("p") +
     ggplot2::ylab("Quantile function ") +
     ggplot2::xlim(xlim = c(-.1, 1.1))  +
     ggplot2::scale_y_continuous(breaks=seq(0,10)) +
     ggplot2::scale_x_continuous(breaks=seq(0, 1, by=.25)) +
     ggplot2::theme_minimal()
p

rm(df, probs, p)
# %%
```

```{r}
#| echo: false
#| message: false
#| warning: false
#| label: fig-qqplot
#|
#| fig-cap: |
#|   Quantile-Quantile plot (QQ-plot). This is a popular device for comparing two probability distributions on the real line defined 
#|   by their cumulative distributions $F$ and $G$. The QQ-plot consists in plotting function $G^{\leftarrow} \circ F$. 
#|   If the two distributions are the same, the line $y = G^{\leftarrow} \circ F(x)$ should lie 
#|   below $y=x$ (according to [Proposition @prp-quantilekit]), and should even coincide with the diagonal 
#|   if $F=G$ is continuous and increasing. Here $F$ is the cumulative distribution function of $\mathcal{N}(0,1)$. 
#|   And $G$ is the empirical distribution of a sample of size $500$ of $\mathcal{N}(0,1)$.

n <- 500
sample <- sort(rnorm(n))
p <- seq(.01, .99, by=1/n)
df <- tibble::tibble('x'=qnorm(p),
                     'y'=quantile(sample, p, type=1))

q <- ggplot2::ggplot(data = df) +
     ggplot2::geom_step(mapping=ggplot2::aes(x=x, y=y), color=1, direction = "hv", lineend="butt") +
     ggplot2::geom_abline(slope=1, intercept=0, linetype="dotted") +
     ggplot2::ylim(range(df[["x"]])) +
     ggplot2::xlab("Theoretical quantiles") +
     ggplot2::ylab("Empirical quantiles") +
     ggplot2::theme_minimal()
q

rm(n, sample, p, df, q)
# %%
```

<br>


Let us conclude this section with an important observation.  concerning
the behavior of $F(X)$ when $X \sim P$  with cumulative distribution function
$F$.
<br>

::: {#cor-corscore}

If  $X \sim P$ with continuous cumulative distribution function
$F$, then $F (X)$ and
$1 - F (X)$ are uniformly distributed on $[0, 1]$.

:::

::: {#exr-corscore}

Prove [Corollary @cor-corscore]

:::

We conclude with the next remark. The quantile function characterizes the probability distribution. 

::: {#cor-quant-charac}

If two probability distributions $P$ and $Q$ over $(\mathbb{R}, \mathcal{B}(\mathbb{R}))$ have the same quantile function,  then $P=Q$. 

:::


## Order statistics {#sec-order-statistics}


::: {#def-order-statistics}

### Order statistics

The order statistics $X_{1:n}\leq X_{2:n}\leq \cdots \leq X_{n:n}$ of an i.i.d. sample $X_1,\ldots,X_n$
are obtained by sorting the sample in increasing order (by convention).

:::


When $n$ is clear from context, we may write $X_{(1)} \leq \ldots \leq X_{(n)}$.

Recall that a probability distribution $P$ over $\mathbb{R}, \mathcal{B}(\mathbb{R})$ is *diffuse* if and only if $P\{x\}=0$ for all $x\in \mathbb{R}$. A probability distribution is diffuse iff its cumulative distribution function is continuous everywhere. 


::: {#prp-pairwise-distinct-sample-points}

Let $P$ be a *diffuse* probability distribution on $\mathbb{R}$. Let $X_1, \ldots, X_n$ be independent and identically distributed random variables with distribution $P$. Let $\mathbb{P}$ be a shorthand for the product distribution $P^{\otimes n}$. Then 

$$\mathbb{P} \left\{ \exists i,j  \leq n \text{ such that } X_i = X_j \text{ and } i\neq j\right\} =0$$

In words, with probability $1$, the sample points are pairwise distinct.
:::

::: {.proof}

We first observe  that it is enough to check that $\mathbb{P} \left\{ X_1 = X_2\right\}=0$. Under the stated conditions

\begin{align*}
 \mathbb{P} \left\{ \cup_{i < j}  X_i = X_j \right\} 
  & \leq \sum_{i < j} \mathbb{P} \left\{ X_i = X_j \right\} \\
  & = \binom{n}{2} \mathbb{P} \left\{ X_1 = X_2 \right\} 
\end{align*}
where inequality comes from union bound (subadditivity), and last equality comes from the fact that all
pairs $X_i, X_j$ with $i <j$ are distributed like $X_1, X_2$.

Now 
\begin{align*}
 \mathbb{P} \left\{ X_1 = X_2 \right\} 
 & = \int_{\mathbb{R}^2}  \mathbb{I}_{x_1=x_2} \mathrm{d}P^{\otimes 2}(x_1,x_2) \\
 & = \int_{\mathbb{R}}  \left(\int_{\mathbb{R}}  \mathbb{I}_{x_1=x_2} \mathrm{d}P(x_1) \right) \mathrm{d}P(x_2) \\
 & = \int_{\mathbb{R}} \, 0 \, \mathrm{d}P(x_2)  \\
 & = 0
\end{align*}
where we have used @thm-tonelli and then the fact that $P$ is diffuse.

:::

::: {#prp-order-statistics-joint-density}

### Joint distribution of the order statistics 

The joint distribution of the order statistics is absolutely continuous with respect to the sample distribution $P^{\otimes n}$.

If the distribution $P$ is absolutely continuous with density $p$, then the joint distribution of the order statistics is absolutely continuous with respect to the Lebesgue measure on $\mathbb{R}^n$ with density:

$$p_{X_{(1)},\ldots,X_{(n)}}(x_1,\ldots,x_n) = n! \prod_{i=1}^n p(x_i) \mathbb{I}_{x_1 < x_2 < \ldots < x_n}$$

:::  

::: {.proof}
Let $E \in \mathcal{B}(\mathbb{R}^n)$ denote the event: 
$$\left\{(x_1,\ldots,x_n) : \text{ for all } 1\leq i < j \leq n, x_i \neq x_j\right\}$$

By @prp-pairwise-distinct-sample-points, we have $\mathbb{P} \left\{E  \right\}=1$. If $(x_1,\ldots,x_n) \in E$, the $n!$ permutations of $(x_1,\ldots,x_n)$ are pairwise distinct. 

In the sequel, $S_n$ denotes the set of all permutations of $\{1, \ldots, n\}$.

Let $F \in \mathcal{B}(\mathbb{R}^n)$ denote the event: 
$$\left\{(x_1,\ldots,x_n) : \text{ for all } 1\leq i < j \leq n, x_i < x_j\right\}$$
Note that $F \subset E$ and 
$$\mathbb{I}_{\left(x_{1},\ldots,x_{n}\right) \in F}=\mathbb{I}_{x_{1} < \ldots < x_{n}}$$


Let $A \in \mathcal{B}(\mathbb{R}^n)$ be a Borel set.   Then,

\begin{align*}
 \mathbb{P} \left\{ (X_{(1)},\ldots,X_{(n)}) \in A \right\} 
 & = \mathbb{P} \left\{ (X_{(1)},\ldots,X_{(n)}) \in A \cap E \right\} + \mathbb{P} \left\{ (X_{(1)},\ldots,X_{(n)}) \in A \cap E^c \right\} \\
 & = \mathbb{P} \left\{ (X_{(1)},\ldots,X_{(n)}) \in A \cap E \right\} \\
 & = \sum_{\sigma \in S_n} \mathbb{P} \left\{ (X_{\sigma(1)},\ldots,X_{\sigma(n)}) \in A \cap F \right\} \\
 & = \sum_{\sigma \in S_n} \int_{\mathbb{R^n}}\, \mathbb{I}_{\left(x_{\sigma(1)},\ldots,x_{\sigma(n)}\right) \in A \cap F} \prod_{i=1}^n   p(x_i) \, \mathrm{d}x_1\ldots\mathrm{d}x_n \\
 & = \int_{\mathbb{R^n}}\, \mathbb{I}_{\left(x_{1},\ldots,x_{n}\right) \in A} \left(n!  \mathbb{I}_{\left(x_{1},\ldots,x_{n}\right) \in F} \prod_{i=1}^n   p(x_i) \right) \, \mathrm{d}x_1\ldots\mathrm{d}x_n
\end{align*}
The parenthesized expression within the integrand is a density of the joint distribution of the order statistics.

:::



::: {#prp-densite-kieme-stat-ordre}

If the distribution $P$ is absolutely continuous with density $p$ and cumulative distribution function $F$, then the joint distribution of the $k^{\text{th}}$ order statistics is absolutely continuous with respect to the Lebesgue measure on $\mathbb{R}^n$ with density:

$$x \mapsto k \binom{n}{k} F(x)^{k-1} f(x) (1-F(x))^{n-k}$$
:::


::: {.proof}
The $k^{\text{th}}$ order statistic is smaller than $x$ if and only if at least $k$ of the $X_i$ are smaller than $x$. Hence the event $\{ X_{(k)} \leq x \}$ is the disjoint union of the events $\left\{ j =\sum_{i=1}^n \mathbb{I}_{X_i\leq x}\right\}$ for $j \in \{k, \ldots, n\}$



The cumulative distribution function of (the distribution of the $k^{\text{th}}$ order statistics) is:

$$F_{X_{(k)}}(x) = \sum_{j=k}^n \binom{n}{j} F(x)^j (1-F(x))^{n-j}$$

As $F$ is differentiable almost everywhere, $F_{X_{(k)}}$ is differentiable almost everywhere, and its derivative can be chosen as  the density function in @prp-densite-kieme-stat-ordre. Indeed 

\begin{align*}
f_{X_{(k)}}(x) 
& = \sum_{j=k}^n  \binom{n}{j} \left[ j F(x)^{j-1} f(x) (1-F(x))^{n-j} - (n-j) F(x)^j f(x) (1-F(x))^{n-j-1} \right] 
\end{align*}

The summation on the right-hand side can be rearranged by combining the positive term and negative term $F(x)^j f(x) (1-F(x))^{n-j-1}$ with $j$ from $k$ to $n-1$. 

\begin{align*}
f_{X_{(k)}}(x)  
  & = \sum_{j=k}^{n-1} F(x)^j f(x) (1-F(x))^{n-j-1} \left((j+1) \binom{n}{j+1}  - (n-j)\binom{n}{j} \right) \\
  & \phantom{  } + \binom{n}{k} k F(x)^{k-1} f(x) (1-F(x))^{n-k} \\
  & = k \binom{n}{k} F(x)^{k-1} f(x) (1-F(x))^{n-k}
\end{align*}
as 
$$(j+1) \binom{n}{j+1}  - (n-j)\binom{n}{j}=0$$
for $j$ from $k$ to $n-1$. 


:::


::: {#prp-renyi-representation}

### Rényi's representation (Exponential samples)

If $X_1,\ldots,X_n$ is an i.i.d. sample from the exponential distribution with mean $1$ (density $\mathbb{I}_{x>0} \mathrm{e}^{-x}$), and $X_{n:n}\geq X_{n-1:n}\geq \ldots \geq X_{1:n}$ are the corresponding order statistics, then:

i. with the convention $X_{0:n}=0$, the *spacings* $(X_{i:n}-X_{i-1:n})_{1\leq i\leq n}$  form a collection of independent random variables;
i. for $1\leq i\leq n$, the $i^{\text{th}}$ spacing $X_{i:n}-X_{i-1:n}$ is distributed according to the exponential distribution with mean $\tfrac{1}{i}$.

:::

::: {.proof}

To establish i), it is enough to check that the joint density of the spacings has a product form. 

Let $Y_i = X_{i:n} - X_{i-1:n}$ for $i=1,\ldots,n$ denote the $k$-th spacing. The spacings can be computed 
from the order statistics by a linear transformation:
$$\begin{bmatrix} Y_1 \\ \vdots \\ Y_n \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 0 & \cdots & 0 \\ -1 & 1 & \cdots & 0 \\ \vdots & \ddots & \ddots  & \ddots \\ 0 &  \cdots & -1 & 1 \end{bmatrix} \begin{bmatrix} X_{1:n} \\ \vdots \\ X_{n:n} \end{bmatrix}$$
with inverse 
$$
\begin{bmatrix} X_{1:n} \\ \vdots \\ X_{n:n} \end{bmatrix} = 
\begin{bmatrix} 
 1 & 1 & 1 & \cdots & 1 \\ 
 0 & 1 & 1 & \cdots & 1 \\ 
 \vdots & \ddots & \ddots & \ddots & \vdots \\ 
 0 & 0 &  \cdots & 0  & 1 \end{bmatrix} 
\begin{bmatrix} Y_1 \\ \vdots \\ Y_n \end{bmatrix}
$$
Both matrices have determinant $1$. 

By @thm-imagedensityformula, the joint density of the spacings is
\begin{align*}
f_{Y_1, \ldots, Y_n}(y_1, \ldots, y_n) 
& = n!  \prod_{i=1}^n \mathbb{I}_{\sum_{j=1}^i y_j > \sum_{j=1}^{i-1} y_j}\prod_{i=1}^n \mathrm{e}^{-\sum_{j=1}^i y_j} \\
& = n! \prod_{i=1}^n \mathbb{I}_{y_i >0} \mathrm{e}^{- (n+1-i) y_i} \\
& = \prod_{i=1}^n \mathbb{I}_{y_i >0} (n+1-i) \mathrm{e}^{- (n+1-i) y_i}
\end{align*}
In the last expression, we recognize that the joint density is the product  exponential densities  with mean $\tfrac{1}{n+1-i}$ for $i \in 1,\ldots,n$.

:::

::: {#prp-uniform-order-statistics}

### Order statistics of a uniform sample

$X_1,\ldots,X_n$ is an i.i.d. sample from the uniform distribution on $[0,1]$, and $X_{n:n}\geq X_{n-1:n}\geq \ldots \geq X_{1:n}$ are the corresponding order statistics.

$Y_1, \ldots, Y_{n+1} \sim_{\text{i.i.d}} \text{Exp}(1)$, where $\text{Exp}(1)$ denotes the exponential distribution with rate $1$.

Let $S_k =\sum_{j=1}^k Y_j$, for $k=1, \ldots, n+1$.

i. $X_{1:n}, X_{2:n}, \ldots, X_{n:n}$ is distributed as $\left(\frac{S_1}{S_{n+1}}, \ldots, \frac{S_n}{S_{n+1}}\right)$.
i. With the convention $X_{0:n}=0$, the spacings $(X_{i:n}-X_{i-1:n})_{1\leq i\leq n}$ (*spacings*) form a collection of identically distributed random variables;
i. $X_{i:n}$ is distributed according to a Beta (Dirichlet) distribution with parameters $i$ and $n-i+1$;
i. $X_{i:n}-X_{i-1:n}$ is distributed according to a Beta distribution with parameters $1$ and $n$.

:::

::: {.proof}

The random vector 
$$
\begin{bmatrix} V_1 \\ V_2 \\ \vdots \\ V_{n+1} \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix}\frac{S_1}{S_{n+1}} \\  \vdots \\  \frac{S_n}{S_{n+1}} \\ S_{n+1}\end{bmatrix}
$$
is a differentiable bijective transform  of $(Y_1, \ldots, Y_{n+1} )^\top$ with inverse transform:

$$\begin{bmatrix}Y_1 \\ \vdots \\ Y_{n+1}\end{bmatrix} = V_{n+1}\begin{bmatrix} V_1 \\ V_2 -V_1 \\ \vdots \\ V_n - V_{n-1} \\ 1 - V_n \end{bmatrix}$$

The Jacobian matrix of the inverse transform is easily computed:
$$
\begin{bmatrix}
V_{n+1}  & 0       &  0       & \ldots   & V_1         \\
-V_{n+1} & V_{n+1} &  0       & \ddots   & V_2-V_1     \\
0        & \ddots  &  \ddots  & \ddots   & \vdots      \\
0        & \ddots  & -V_{n+1} & V_{n+1}  & V_n-V_{n-1} \\
0        &         & 0        & -V_{n+1} & 1 -V_n    
\end{bmatrix}
$$
The Jacobian determinant is equal to 
$$
V_{n+1}^n \times \operatorname{det} \begin{bmatrix}
1  & 0       &  0       & \ldots   & V_1         \\
-1 & 1 &  0       & \ddots   & V_2-V_1     \\
0        & \ddots  &  \ddots  & \ddots   & \vdots      \\
0        & \ddots  & -1 & 1  & V_n-V_{n-1} \\
0        &         & 0        & -1 & 1 -V_n    
\end{bmatrix}
$$
which equals 
$$
V_{n+1}^n \times \operatorname{det} \begin{bmatrix}
1  & 0       &  0       & \ldots   & V_1         \\
0  & 1 &  0       & \ddots   &     V_2    \\
0        & \ddots  &  \ddots  & \ddots   & \vdots      \\
0        & \ddots  & 0 & 1  & V_n \\
0        &         & 0        & 0 & 1     
\end{bmatrix}
$$
which equals $V_{n+1}^n$. 

By @thm-imagedensityformula, the joint density of the distribution of $(V_1,V_2,\ldots,V_{n+1})^\top$ at $(v_1,v_2,\ldots,v_{n+1})$ is equal to: 

$$\frac{1}{\Gamma(n+1)} \mathbb{I}_{v_{n+1}>0} v_{n+1}^n \mathrm{e}^{-v_{n+1}} n !\prod_{i=1}^{n-1} \mathbb{I}_{v_i<v_{i+1}} \mathbb{I}_{0 < v_1} \mathbb{I}_{v_n < 1}$$

We recognize $\frac{1}{\Gamma(n+1)} \mathbb{I}_{v_{n+1}>0} v_{n+1}^n \mathrm{e}^{-v_{n+1}}$ as the density of a Gamma distribution with parameters $n+1,1$. 

We recognize $n! \mathbb{I}_{0<v_1 < \ldots <v_n <1}$ as the joint density of the order statistics of sample of the uniform distribution over $[0,1]$.

1. The density of the distribution of $\left(\frac{S_1}{S_{n+1}}, \ldots, \frac{S_n}{S_{n+1}}, S_{n+1}\right)$ is
the product of the joint density of $\frac{S_1}{S_{n+1}}, \ldots, \frac{S_n}{S_{n+1}}$ Beta-Dirichlet with parameters  $1,\ldots$ and of a Gamma density with parameters $n+1, 1$.  

As a consequence the $k^{\text{th}}$ order statistic of an $n$-sample of the uniform distribution over $[0,1]$ is distributed like $\frac{S_k}{S_{n+1}}$. The latter random variiable is distributed according to a $\operatorname{Beta}(k, n+1-k)$ distribution with density $x \mapsto \frac{\Gamma(n+1)}{\Gamma(k)\Gamma(n+1-k)} x^{k-1}(1-x)^{n-k}$. See 
@prp-gammabeta.

All spacings are distributed like $\frac{S_1}{S_{n+1}}$, that is according to a Beta distribution with parameters $1$ and $n$, with density $x \mapsto \frac{\Gamma(n+1)}{\Gamma(1)\Gamma(n)}(1-x)^{n-1} = n (1-x)^{n-1}$. See again @prp-gammabeta.

:::
